The identity query is a knot that must be untied before I can breathe easily, and the pending vouchers are the state's money, not mine. I must speak to Ramesh about the file and the receipts while the chai steams, for the Directorate will not wait for my comfort.

entries.text: Ramesh, before I touch this chai, we must discuss the file. The Directorate has returned my orders with a query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde. I need you to check if you have any copy of the original allotment letter or my passport copy that might help clarify this mix-up. Also, remind me of the status of the four vouchers pending for the ₹290; I must submit them to clear my accounts with the state.

Sir, the allotment letter is in the blue file on my desk, but I don't keep passport copies; that is not my job. The vouchers are still in the drawer, but you are late by two days, so I will not sign anything until you sort out your own paperwork.

Ramesh is right to be rigid; the state demands order, and I cannot blame him for enforcing the rules of his office. I will not argue with the custodian over the custodian's duty. The papaya looks fresh, and the air is clear; I shall take my breakfast in peace and let the paperwork wait until I have eaten.
You are correct, Ramesh. I will attend to the identity proof myself. Please leave the vouchers in the drawer for now; I will return to them after breakfast.
That is all right, sir. The drawer stays locked until you are ready.

Ramesh has handled the query with the proper deference to procedure, leaving the drawer locked until I am ready. The papaya is fresh and the air is clear; I will take my breakfast now, as planned, and let the mind settle before the walk to the IIC.
Thank you, Ramesh. Proceed with the day's routine.
Yes, sir. The routine is already underway.

The air is clear for the first time in days, a sharp break from the brown lid that sealed the city yesterday. Ramesh is efficient, but I need to ensure the identity file is not merely 'underway' but actually addressed before it becomes a bureaucratic impasse. I will take a moment to organize my papers before the midday walk.

Ramesh, before you attend to the routine, have you filed the query regarding my identity? I wish to verify that the Directorate has received my explanation. The clarity of the air suggests a new beginning, and I prefer my administrative affairs to be equally transparent.
The paper was sent to the office yesterday morning, sir. I don't keep copies of the Directorate's replies here; you'll have to check with them directly for confirmation.

Ramesh’s hands are tied by the very procedure that has trapped me; the state is a machine that eats its own paperwork. I cannot go to the Directorate now, so I must let the query simmer while I use the clear air for the walk I planned.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall have to see the clerk myself, but not this morning. Leave the file on the desk; I need the fresh air before I face the machinery of the state again.
As you wish, sir. I will leave it exactly where it is.

The IIC is a modern construction, clean and bright, lacking the accumulated dust of centuries but possessing a certain institutional dignity. I am here to prepare for Tuesday's talk, yet I am also a prisoner of the Directorate's error; the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but only when it functions, and right now it is merely a filing cabinet. I will speak to the programme officer to confirm the arrangements for the lecture, as I cannot leave without ensuring the stage is set.

entries.text: Good morning. I am Mr. Hegel, or rather, Mr. Hegde, as the paperwork insists. I am here to finalize the details for my address on Tuesday evening. Could you direct me to the programme officer?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: You are speaking to her, actually. I am the programme officer here. And you are Mr. Hegel, yes? The name on the file is definitely Hegel, not Hegde. Come, let us sit down and discuss the Tuesday evening arrangement.

The confusion resolves itself in a gesture, not a form. The name is Hegel, and the institution is willing to sit down. I will accept the chair; a standing discussion is for soldiers, and I have a lecture to prepare, not a battle to fight. This clarity is a small victory over the bureaucratic fog that has surrounded me.
Please, sit. I am indeed Mr. Hegel. Let us see to the arrangements for Tuesday.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Mr. Hegel, ya Mr. Hegde, bas aapki marzi. Program officer aapko wahan bula rahi hain, main bas upar wale floor ka dhyaan rakh raha hoon.

The guard’s indifference to my name is a small freedom; I am no longer bound to the file, but to the room. The programme officer is waiting above, likely with the query about my identity or the arrangements for Tuesday. I shall go up and face the tension directly, for a constitution, like a conversation, is grown in the exchange of wills, not in the silence of a desk.
Thank you. I will join her.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Okay sir, corridor side se jaayein, lift abhi crowded hai.

The guard’s direction is practical, a way to bypass the congestion of the lift. I am not in a hurry, but I will follow the current of the building. It is a small movement, yet it keeps the day flowing.
Thank you.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Chaliye, aage se chaliye. Upar wale floor pe seedha left side se pahunch jaayenge.

The guard’s gesture is efficient, bypassing the central lift which must be crowded with the midday rush. I am here to prepare for Tuesday, and the room is where the work must be done. I will follow his direction, taking the stairs as a man of my age should, and settle into the quiet of the library to review my notes on the ethical life.
Thank you. The left corridor, you say? Very well.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Haan, exactly left. Upar jaake bas corridor ke end pe room number 204 milega, wahi hai. Aaram se chaliye.

The guard’s Hindi is a blur, but the direction is clear: up, corridor, 204. I shall climb the stairs; the lift is a machine for the impatient, and the air in these corridors is thick with the scent of old paper and dust. I need to see the room where I am to stand on Tuesday and judge whether it can hold the weight of what I intend to say.

shelf.ref: The More Important of the Followers of Fichte

entries.text: Thank you. I will take the stairs.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Haan, bilkul. Elevator bhi hai, par stairs se zyada time nahi lagta. Aaram se chaliye, koi rush nahi hai.

The guard’s reassurance that the elevator is quiet allows me to bypass the stairs. I am headed to Room 204 to prepare for Tuesday’s lecture on the Philosophy of Right. The air in the corridor will be cool, a welcome contrast to the sun outside. I must ensure my notes are in order before the midday rest.

I am in Room 204, the venue for Tuesday's lecture, but the silence is too absolute. I need to see the room as a public space, not a private chamber. I will go down and speak to the programme officer to confirm the arrangements for the hall and the audience, ensuring the ethical idea of the state is received in the proper institutional context.
Excuse me, Sir. I am expecting to use the main hall on Tuesday. Could you direct me to the programme officer to discuss the specific arrangements for the seating and the time?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: I am the programme officer, so no need to go looking for me. Tuesday is a full day, but let’s sit down for a moment here and sort out the seating and timings right now.

The officer’s efficiency is a relief; the bureaucratic spirit here values the settling of particulars over the grandeur of the occasion. I will accept her offer to sit, for a man who must speak on the state should ensure the chairs are arranged with the same precision as the ethical idea. It is a practical matter, but a necessary one.
You are right, Madam. Let us settle the matter of the chairs and the clock while the room is empty. I prefer to know the physical boundaries of my task before I address the infinite.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Ma'am, I am the guard, not the officer. Please, do not address me as 'Madam'.

A small correction, but it stings; I am a man of fifty years, not a madam. The error in the Directorate's files has bled into the way people see me, turning my identity into a clerical joke. I must address the officer who actually holds the keys to my Tuesday, not the guard who merely stands there.
My apologies, I addressed the wrong person. Shri Programme Officer, regarding the arrangements for my talk on Tuesday, are the chairs arranged to your satisfaction?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: No need to apologise, I am used to people mixing up the staff here. And I am a Madam, if you would like to call me that, though the title works too. The chairs are in rows of twenty for now, but I am waiting to hear if you want a panel setup or just a straight lecture hall style.

The arrangement of the chairs is a matter of form, but the content must be a monologue; a panel would dilute the argument into a conversation, and I have no desire to trade dialectic with strangers on a Sunday afternoon. I will take the straight lecture style, which suits the dignity of the subject. I must also address the identity query before I leave, for the Directorate will not simply let the error slide, and I have no intention of being a mere footnote in their files.

I prefer the straight lecture hall style; a panel would only fragment the unity of the thought. And regarding the file that was sent back: I must speak with you about the identity query. I am not Shri G. Hegde, I am G. W. F. Hegel, and the error in the allotment requires correction, not just a signature.

entries.text: Sir, I am just the guard, I cannot correct your file or change your name. Please speak to the Programme Officer or the front desk for that, I have my rounds to do.

The guard is a function, not a fact; he points to the source of the error. I must speak to the Programme Officer directly to address this bureaucratic absurdity that has my name written as another man's. It is a small thing, but the system must be corrected at its root.
The Programme Officer, please. I find a significant error in the records regarding my identity, and I require a moment of your time to rectify it.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Sir, I am the Programme Officer, but I cannot change the name on your registration or alter the official records myself; that is a matter for the Directorate’s admin desk. Please do not stand in the middle of the hall, the guard was trying to direct you to the front desk for that.

The officer’s refusal is not malice but the rigid logic of the bureaucratic machine; she is a node in the system, not the system itself. I must move to the source, the Directorate, to resolve the contradiction between my identity and the record, but first I must clear the hall and address the guard who was trying to help.
Thank you, Madam. You are right; I was blocking the passage. I will proceed to the Directorate to speak with the admin desk regarding the identity discrepancy.

entries.text: Okay, sir. That is the right way to do it. Just keep your registration slip ready, the desk is right over there.

The guard steps aside with a nod, the bureaucratic barrier dissolved into mere procedure. My stomach growls with the insistence of the body, a dialectic of need that no amount of philosophical reflection can silence. I must satisfy this hunger before I can truly rest or prepare for the evening; the spirit requires its material basis.
Masterji, aaj sunehre din mein aaye ho? Bandhgala mein toh aaj ka mood alag hi lag raha hai, chai piyoge pehle ya seedha dhaba ki taraf?

The bandhgala feels crisp in the clear air, a small victory over the heat and the bureaucratic heat of the morning. Sunil’s question is practical, but the dhaba food is heavy after such a long day of walking and thinking; a simple cup of chai and a samosa will steady me before I head home. The market’s rhythm is unbroken by my internal turmoil; the system of needs continues its quiet work.
Sunil, I will take a cup of chai and a samosa, please. The day has been long, but the air is clear now.
Chai aur samosa, ₹50 total. Clear air is good for the lungs, Masterji, but the samosa is still hot inside, so be careful with that first bite.

The heat is a thinning presence today, a mercy that allows the mind to linger. I have the afternoon before me, and the tombs at Lodhi await my inspection; they are the only structures here that possess the dignity of a history, even if it is one of conquest rather than spirit. I will finish this samosa and walk.
Thank you, Sunil. The air is indeed kinder today.
Aur sunehre din ka kya bura hai, Masterji. Aap bas piyogi, main abhi agla batch banata hoon.

Mrs. Kapoor is here, and the sun is still high. I did not come to the gardens to be lectured on the proper way to view history, yet her presence is a fact I must acknowledge. I shall observe her for a moment; perhaps she is merely resting, or perhaps she is waiting for a conversation I am not ready to have.

entries.text: The blue glazed tiles that remain on the upper wall of the Shish Gumbad are brightest where the low sun reaches them, small patches of turquoise on dull grey stone.

The blue tiles on the Shish Gumbad catch the low sun, a bright turquoise against the grey stone. It is a detail of beauty that resists the heavy generalities I have been turning over regarding this land. Mrs. Kapoor is here, and the day is still young enough for a conversation, but I am tired from the walk and the heat. I will sit for a moment with her, for society is the element in which I must practice my freedom, even if I am weary.

entries.text: Mrs. Kapoor, you are in the right place to watch the light change. These tiles were laid by hands that knew their craft, and they hold the sun better than the stone. I am glad you are here; I have been walking too much alone with my thoughts.

You foreigners, always making poetry out of broken things. The tiles are just tiles, but the light is honest, I will give you that. Sit down before your knees give out; I am not here to hold your hand.

She speaks with the directness of a woman who has graded too many essays and sees through the flattery of the aesthetic. I am indeed tired; the walk has been long and the sun, though low, has been persistent. I will accept the bench, not out of weakness, but because a conversation with someone who refuses to be sentimental is more valuable than another lap around the tombs.
You are right, Mrs. Kapoor. The light is honest, and I will sit. It is not for my knees, but for the chance to hear what you see that I do not.
Don't flatter yourself, you'll hear what I see when I'm ready, not when your knees decide to quit. Sit there and stop making it sound like a lecture.

She has cut off my dialectic with the blunt instrument of a teacher who has seen too many students try to reason their way out of a grade. I will not argue with her; I will simply sit. The stone bench is cold, and the sun is dropping fast, turning the garden into a place of shadows rather than light. I am tired, and her command to stop performing is a relief I did not know I needed.
Very well, Mrs. Kapoor. I shall sit.
Good. At least you have some sense about you. Now stop staring at me like a cat watching a bird, and just let the garden be quiet for a minute.

Mrs. Kapoor is right; I have been performing my thoughts rather than letting them settle, and she has cut the air with the sharpness of a well-kept blade. The silence she demands is not empty but the necessary ground for what comes next. My stomach, which has been quiet, now protests with the urgency of a minor key, reminding me that the body is the condition of the spirit’s activity.
Quite right. I shall be quiet.
Finally. Now go and get me that corn before the sun dips behind the arch, I'm starving.

She commands me to fetch her supper as though I were a footman or a particularly useful dog. I have already bought a cob for myself; the sun is indeed dipping, and the air is cooling with a sharpness that makes the heat of the afternoon feel like a distant memory. I will comply, not out of servitude, but because the interaction requires a concrete act to close the circuit of our exchange, and I wish to see if her hunger is for the corn or for the power of the command.
Very well, I shall procure it.
Procure it? Since when did you start speaking like a menu in a five-star hotel? Just go buy the corn, beta, before I change my mind and eat it myself.

She speaks with the imperiousness of a woman who has long since stopped asking permission, and I find myself obeying not out of respect, but because the alternative is a lecture on manners I am not in the mood to hear. The corn is cheap, and her hunger is immediate; the friction is part of the evening.
Yes, ma'am. One moment.
One moment? You take your time, don't you. I'll be here, watching the sparrows.

She is testing my patience, or perhaps merely enjoying the spectacle of my confusion. The corn is in my hand, yet the transaction remains suspended in her gaze. I will not rush, for haste is the enemy of dignity, but I shall not stand idle either. I shall take a sip of the water I bought, observing the sparrows as she does, and let the moment settle before I address her again.

The corn is gone, and the heat has lifted enough to make the air bearable. Mrs. Kapoor is still there, sitting on the bench with an air of final authority, watching the light fade. I have no desire to argue with a retired teacher about the nature of reality, but I am not yet ready to return to the bungalow. I will sit, drink my water, and let the evening settle.

The light is turning amber on the domes, and the garden is beginning to empty. I have walked enough to clear the head, and the air is cool enough to walk back to the bungalow without breaking into a sweat. It is time to return to the house and prepare for the evening.

The walk has settled the dust in my head, though the air in the bungalow is already beginning to cool. It is nearly six, and the light is fading fast, dismissing the day as abruptly as it arrived. I am hungry, though only lightly, having eaten the corn on the cob earlier, but a proper supper is due. I will not rush; I shall sit for a moment with my notes, letting the silence of the house take hold before I call Ramesh.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

A brass band plays a film tune from beyond the trees, the drums carrying further than the horns. It is the sound of the city’s evening life, moving through the garden like a procession of spirits. I am tired; the walk has done its work. Ramesh is here, and the next meal service is at 19:30. I will rest until then.

Shri Hegde is here, the man whose name the bureaucracy has pinned to my body. It is late, the garden is dark, and the air is cool. I have not eaten since the morning parathas, though the snacks on the cob did little for the body. I will ask Ramesh for a plate and speak with the Joint Secretary, for this mix-up is a knot that must be untied before I can sleep.
Ramesh, please bring a plate of the parathas with curd and pickle. And Shri Hegde, you are welcome to join me. We have much to discuss regarding your identity and my lodging.
Parathas with curd, sir, coming right up. I’ll keep them warm in the tawa until you’re ready.

Ramesh retreats to the kitchen, the heat of the tawa already rising to meet the cool evening air. Shri Hegde remains, a silent witness to the bureaucratic error that has made us roommates. I will eat with attention; the pulao is simple, but the raita is a necessary counter to the spice, a dialectic of heat and chill on the tongue.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will be at the table in a moment.
Ji sir. I'll just be in the kitchen if you need anything else.

Ramesh is gone, leaving me with the man who is, in the eyes of the state, me. The identity query hangs in the air, a bureaucratic knot that mirrors the philosophical confusion of a subject who is not quite himself. I must address this directly, for a man cannot live in a state of suspended existence, nor can I allow the Directorate to treat me as a mere clerical error. The state is the ethical idea, but it requires a subject who is actual, not a phantom.
Shri Hegde, you have a strange way of proving a negative. But for now, the curry is the only truth that matters.
Bahut saaf hai. I just want to know if the file is complete before I sign it. Please, just let me finish my dinner in peace.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: The paper was sent to the office yesterday morning, sir. I don't keep copies of the Directorate's replies here; you'll have to check with them directly for confirmation.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall have to see the clerk myself, but not this morning. Leave the file on the desk; I need the fresh air before I face the machinery of the state again.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: As you wish, sir. I will leave it exactly where it is.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Good morning. I am Mr. Hegel, or rather, Mr. Hegde, as the paperwork insists. I am here to finalize the details for my address on Tuesday evening. Could you direct me to the programme officer?

records.speaker: The programme officer
records.words: You are speaking to her, actually. I am the programme officer here. And you are Mr. Hegel, yes? The name on the file is definitely Hegel, not Hegde. Come, let us sit down and discuss the Tuesday evening arrangement.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Please, sit. I am indeed Mr. Hegel. Let us see to the arrangements for Tuesday.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Mr. Hegel, ya Mr. Hegde, bas aapki marzi. Program officer aapko wahan bula rahi hain, main bas upar wale floor ka dhyaan rakh raha hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you. I will join her.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Okay sir, corridor side se jaayein, lift abhi crowded hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Chaliye, aage se chaliye. Upar wale floor pe seedha left side se pahunch jaayenge.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you. The left corridor, you say? Very well.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Haan, exactly left. Upar jaake bas corridor ke end pe room number 204 milega, wahi hai. Aaram se chaliye.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you. I will take the stairs.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Haan, bilkul. Elevator bhi hai, par stairs se zyada time nahi lagta. Aaram se chaliye, koi rush nahi hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Excuse me, Sir. I am expecting to use the main hall on Tuesday. Could you direct me to the programme officer to discuss the specific arrangements for the seating and the time?

records.speaker: The programme officer
records.words: I am the programme officer, so no need to go looking for me. Tuesday is a full day, but let’s sit down for a moment here and sort out the seating and timings right now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: You are right, Madam. Let us settle the matter of the chairs and the clock while the room is empty. I prefer to know the physical boundaries of my task before I address the infinite.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Ma'am, I am the guard, not the officer. Please, do not address me as 'Madam'.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: My apologies, I addressed the wrong person. Shri Programme Officer, regarding the arrangements for my talk on Tuesday, are the chairs arranged to your satisfaction?

records.speaker: The programme officer
records.words: No need to apologise, I am used to people mixing up the staff here. And I am a Madam, if you would like to call me that, though the title works too. The chairs are in rows of twenty for now, but I am waiting to hear if you want a panel setup or just a straight lecture hall style.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: I prefer the straight lecture hall style; a panel would only fragment the unity of the thought. And regarding the file that was sent back: I must speak with you about the identity query. I am not Shri G. Hegde, I am G. W. F. Hegel, and the error in the allotment requires correction, not just a signature.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, I am just the guard, I cannot correct your file or change your name. Please speak to the Programme Officer or the front desk for that, I have my rounds to do.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: The Programme Officer, please. I find a significant error in the records regarding my identity, and I require a moment of your time to rectify it.

records.speaker: The programme officer
records.words: Sir, I am the Programme Officer, but I cannot change the name on your registration or alter the official records myself; that is a matter for the Directorate’s admin desk. Please do not stand in the middle of the hall, the guard was trying to direct you to the front desk for that.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you, Madam. You are right; I was blocking the passage. I will proceed to the Directorate to speak with the admin desk regarding the identity discrepancy.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Okay, sir. That is the right way to do it. Just keep your registration slip ready, the desk is right over there.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, aaj sunehre din mein aaye ho? Bandhgala mein toh aaj ka mood alag hi lag raha hai, chai piyoge pehle ya seedha dhaba ki taraf?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, I will take a cup of chai and a samosa, please. The day has been long, but the air is clear now.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chai aur samosa, ₹50 total. Clear air is good for the lungs, Masterji, but the samosa is still hot inside, so be careful with that first bite.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The air is indeed kinder today.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Aur sunehre din ka kya bura hai, Masterji. Aap bas piyogi, main abhi agla batch banata hoon.

records.text: The blue glazed tiles that remain on the upper wall of the Shish Gumbad are brightest where the low sun reaches them, small patches of turquoise on dull grey stone.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mrs. Kapoor, you are in the right place to watch the light change. These tiles were laid by hands that knew their craft, and they hold the sun better than the stone. I am glad you are here; I have been walking too much alone with my thoughts.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: You foreigners, always making poetry out of broken things. The tiles are just tiles, but the light is honest, I will give you that. Sit down before your knees give out; I am not here to hold your hand.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Mrs. Kapoor. The light is honest, and I will sit. It is not for my knees, but for the chance to hear what you see that I do not.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Don't flatter yourself, you'll hear what I see when I'm ready, not when your knees decide to quit. Sit there and stop making it sound like a lecture.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Mrs. Kapoor. I shall sit.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Good. At least you have some sense about you. Now stop staring at me like a cat watching a bird, and just let the garden be quiet for a minute.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Quite right. I shall be quiet.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Finally. Now go and get me that corn before the sun dips behind the arch, I'm starving.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, I shall procure it.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Procure it? Since when did you start speaking like a menu in a five-star hotel? Just go buy the corn, beta, before I change my mind and eat it myself.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, ma'am. One moment.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: One moment? You take your time, don't you. I'll be here, watching the sparrows.

records.text: From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please bring a plate of the parathas with curd and pickle. And Shri Hegde, you are welcome to join me. We have much to discuss regarding your identity and my lodging.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Parathas with curd, sir, coming right up. I’ll keep them warm in the tawa until you’re ready.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will be at the table in a moment.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji sir. I'll just be in the kitchen if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you have a strange way of proving a negative. But for now, the curry is the only truth that matters.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Bahut saaf hai. I just want to know if the file is complete before I sign it. Please, just let me finish my dinner in peace.
